why: Every project manager, IT project manager and PMO analyst is judged first on the plan: what will be delivered, by when, and what the date depends on. Interviews test it directly (“walk me through how you build a schedule”, “what is the critical path?”), and on the job a weak plan shows up within weeks as missed dates nobody saw coming.
outcome: write a project charter, define scope with a WBS, estimate with analogous, parametric and three-point (PERT) methods, link tasks with the four dependency types, find the critical path and float with a forward and backward pass, build a Gantt chart with milestones and levelled resources, and track progress against a baseline.

lessons.title: What a project manager does, and which life cycle to use
text: PMI defines a project as a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result. Temporary means it has a start and an end; unique means it has not been done in exactly this way before. Operations are the opposite: the ongoing, repeated work that keeps the business running, such as running the payroll every month or answering support tickets. Moving a company’s payroll to a new software package is a project; running that payroll afterwards is operations.

The project manager is accountable for delivering the agreed result within the agreed constraints: scope, time and cost (the “triple constraint” or iron triangle), with quality, risks and the people involved around them. Change one side and the others move: adding scope without adding time or money puts the date or the quality at risk. The PM does not do all the work; they plan it, organise who does it, track it, remove blockers, manage risks and changes, and keep the sponsor and stakeholders informed.

A predictive life cycle, often called waterfall, plans the whole project up front and runs it in phases: requirements, design, build, test, deploy. Each phase ends with a deliverable and often a phase gate, a formal go / no-go decision. French teams often speak of the V-model (cycle en V), where each build phase on the left side has a matching test phase on the right. Predictive works well when requirements are stable and well understood, when the work is hard to change late (construction, hardware, a regulated migration) or when a contract fixes scope and price.

An agile life cycle, for example Scrum, delivers in short iterations (sprints of one to four weeks) and re-plans after each one with feedback from users. It suits work where the need will become clearer as people use early versions, such as a new app. Most companies actually run hybrid projects: a predictive frame with fixed milestones, a budget and a go-live date, and agile delivery inside some phases, such as the software build in sprints while the data migration and the training follow a classic plan.

In interviews, avoid presenting one method as always better. Hiring managers want to hear that you choose the life cycle from the project: how stable the requirements are, how costly a late change is, what the contract says and what the organisation is used to. This course focuses on predictive planning tools (charter, WBS, schedule, critical path, baseline), which are also used inside hybrid projects to plan milestones and dependencies.
points: Project: temporary and unique; operations: ongoing and repeated.
Triple constraint: scope, time and cost move together; quality depends on all three.
Predictive (waterfall, V-model): plan up front, phases and phase gates, for stable requirements.
Agile: short iterations and re-planning, for needs that become clear with use.
Hybrid: a predictive frame with milestones, agile delivery inside some phases.

example.code:
Project: replace the payroll software (go-live 1 January)

Life cycle: hybrid
  Predictive frame : charter -> scope -> plan -> build -> parallel run -> go-live
  Phase gates      : G1 scope signed | G2 data migrated | G3 parallel run OK
  Agile inside     : HR portal screens built in 2-week sprints

Operations after go-live: monthly payroll run (not part of the project)
example.note: A fixed date and a legal deadline favour a predictive frame; the part where users must react to screens is delivered in sprints.

lessons.title: The project charter and the business case
text: The business case answers “why should we spend money on this?”. It describes the problem or opportunity, the options considered (including doing nothing), the expected costs, benefits and risks of each, and the recommended option. A useful business case states measurable benefits, for example “reduce manual invoice processing from 6 to 2 days” or “save 120,000 € a year in licences”, so the project can later be checked against them. PRINCE2 makes “continued business justification” one of its principles: if the business case stops holding during the project, the project should be changed or stopped.

The project charter is the document that formally authorises the project and gives the project manager the authority to use resources. It is short, often one to three pages, and is signed by the sponsor, the senior person who owns the business case, funds the project and makes the big decisions. French teams often call it the note de cadrage. A charter typically contains the purpose and objectives, high-level scope, key deliverables, main milestones, summary budget, main risks and assumptions, the success criteria, the sponsor and the project manager, and the key stakeholders.

Objectives in a charter should be SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. “Improve the website” is not an objective; “launch the new checkout by 30 June, with the conversion rate measured at 3.0 % or more over the following month” is one. Success criteria say how the sponsor will decide that the project worked, and they must be agreed before the work starts, not argued about at the end.

The charter is not the detailed plan. It does not contain the task list, the full schedule or each person’s assignments; those come later in the project management plan. A common mistake is to start working without a signed charter because “everyone agrees”: when a conflict appears three months later about scope or budget, nobody can point to what was agreed. Another is a charter so vague that every stakeholder reads their own project into it.

Assumptions and constraints deserve a line each. An assumption is something taken as true without proof (“the vendor API will be available in test by 1 March”); a constraint is a limit you must respect (“budget capped at 250,000 €”, “go-live before the legal deadline”). Writing assumptions down turns them into things to check, and a wrong assumption often becomes a risk or an issue later.
points: Business case: why, options, costs, benefits, risks and a recommendation.
Project charter: authorises the project and names the PM; signed by the sponsor.
SMART objectives and success criteria agreed before the work starts.
The charter is high level; tasks and the detailed schedule go in the plan.
List assumptions (to check) and constraints (to respect).

example.code:
PROJECT CHARTER - New customer portal
Sponsor          : Head of Customer Service
Project manager  : (named here, with authority over the project budget)
Purpose          : let customers download invoices and open tickets online
Objectives       : portal live by 30 June; 40% of invoice requests self-served by 30 Sept
In scope         : invoices, tickets, password reset, FR and EN
Out of scope     : online payment (phase 2), mobile app
Milestones       : design signed 15 Feb | UAT start 2 May | go-live 30 June
Budget           : 180,000 EUR (incl. 10% contingency)
Assumptions      : billing system API available in test by 1 March
Constraints      : GDPR; no change freeze breach in December
Main risks       : API delay; low adoption
Signed           : sponsor, date
example.note: One page the sponsor signs: enough to authorise the work, not the detailed plan.

lessons.title: Scope: requirements, in and out of scope, the WBS
text: Scope is everything the project will deliver, and nothing else. It starts with requirements collected from stakeholders through interviews, workshops, existing documents and observation, then turned into a scope statement: the deliverables, the acceptance criteria for each, what is explicitly out of scope, and the assumptions. In French teams the requirements often arrive as a cahier des charges or an expression de besoin.

The out-of-scope list is as important as the in-scope one. Writing “online payment is out of scope (phase 2)” in black and white prevents months of “I thought it was included”. Scope creep is the slow growth of scope without matching changes to time, budget or resources, often one small request at a time. The answer is not to refuse everything but to send each change through change control: assess the impact on time and cost, then let the sponsor decide.

The work breakdown structure (WBS) decomposes the total scope into smaller, manageable pieces, organised by deliverable. Level 1 is the project, level 2 the main deliverables or phases, and so on down to work packages, the lowest level, which can be estimated, assigned to one owner and tracked. The 100 % rule says that the WBS contains all the work of the project and nothing more: the children of each element add up to exactly 100 % of their parent. Project management itself is usually a branch of the WBS too.

A WBS is a list of deliverables (nouns), not a schedule: it has no dates and no dependencies. The activities (verbs) that produce each work package come next and go into the schedule. A practical rule of thumb used by many PMs, the 8/80 rule, says a work package should take between about 8 and 80 hours of effort, or fit within one reporting period; too large and you cannot track it, too small and you drown in detail. Each work package can be described in a WBS dictionary: description, owner, acceptance criteria, estimate.

In interviews, a common exercise is “draw the WBS for a small event or app”. Start from the deliverables, keep the levels consistent, include project management, testing and training (the most often forgotten branches), and check the 100 % rule by asking “if all these pieces are done, is the project done?”.
points: Scope statement: deliverables, acceptance criteria, out of scope, assumptions.
Write the out-of-scope list explicitly; send every change through change control.
WBS: deliverable-oriented decomposition down to work packages.
100 % rule: all the work, nothing more; project management is a branch too.
Work package: estimable, one owner, trackable (8/80 rule as a guide).

example.code:
1 Customer portal
  1.1 Project management
      1.1.1 Charter and plan
      1.1.2 Status reporting and steering
  1.2 Design
      1.2.1 Requirements and user stories
      1.2.2 UX mock-ups
  1.3 Portal software
      1.3.1 Invoices module
      1.3.2 Tickets module
      1.3.3 Login and password reset
  1.4 Integration with billing API
  1.5 Testing
      1.5.1 System tests
      1.5.2 User acceptance tests (UAT)
  1.6 Deployment and training

      1.6.2 User guides and training
example.note: Nouns, not verbs; no dates. Each lowest line is a work package with one owner.

lessons.title: Estimating: analogous, parametric and three-point (PERT)
text: Estimates answer two questions: how much effort (person-days of work) and how much duration (calendar time). They differ: 10 days of effort done by two people working half time on it takes about 10 working days of duration. Estimate with the people who will do the work, at the work package level, and write down the assumptions behind each number.

Analogous estimating uses a similar past project: “last year’s portal took 40 days of build; this one has about 25 % more screens, so about 50 days”. It is fast and useful early, when little is known, but only as good as the comparison. Parametric estimating uses a unit rate multiplied by a quantity: 120 test cases at 0.25 day each gives 30 days; 2,000 m² of office at a known cost per m². It is more accurate when the rate comes from real data and the work scales roughly linearly.

Three-point estimating asks for three values: optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P). The triangular average is (O + M + P) / 3. The PERT (beta) estimate weights the most likely value: (O + 4M + P) / 6. With O = 10, M = 15 and P = 26 days, PERT gives (10 + 60 + 26) / 6 = 16 days, more than the most likely 15 because the pessimistic tail is longer. A common measure of uncertainty is the standard deviation (P − O) / 6, here 16 / 6 ≈ 2.7 days.

Padding is adding a hidden safety margin to each task (“say 15 when you think 10”). It is a bad habit: the margins are invisible, they get used up anyway (people tend to fill the time available, often called Parkinson’s law), and the plan loses credibility. The better practice is honest task estimates plus an explicit contingency reserve, held at project level, sized from the identified risks, visible to the sponsor and consumed in a controlled way. A management reserve, for unknown unknowns, is usually held by the sponsor outside the PM’s baseline.

Estimates become more accurate as the project progresses, so give ranges early (“8 to 12 weeks”) and refine them. Interviewers often ask how you handle a sponsor who wants a firm date on day one: give a range with the assumptions, explain what would narrow it, and commit to a re-estimate at a set point, for example after the design phase.
points: Effort (person-days) is not duration (calendar days).
Analogous: from a similar past project; parametric: unit rate × quantity.
PERT: (O + 4M + P) / 6; standard deviation (P − O) / 6.
No hidden padding: honest estimates plus a visible contingency reserve.
Give ranges early and refine them as you learn.

example.code:
A                 B (O)  C (M)  D (P)  E (PERT)
1    Task              Opt    Likely Pess   PERT
2    Billing API link  10     15     26     =(B2+4*C2+D2)/6   -> 16
3    Std deviation                          =(D2-B2)/6        -> 2.67
4    Parametric tests  120 cases x 0.25 day = 30 days
example.note: PERT leans towards the most likely value but is pulled up by a long pessimistic tail.

lessons.title: Dependencies and the network diagram
text: A schedule is not a list of tasks with dates typed in: it is a network of activities linked by dependencies, so that when one task moves, everything after it moves too. The precedence diagramming method (PDM), also called activity on node, draws each activity as a box and each dependency as an arrow from predecessor to successor.

There are four dependency types. Finish-to-start (FS), by far the most common: B cannot start until A has finished (the tests start when the build is finished). Start-to-start (SS): B cannot start until A has started (writing the user guide can start once the build has started). Finish-to-finish (FF): B cannot finish until A has finished (the test report cannot be finished until testing is finished). Start-to-finish (SF), rare: B cannot finish until A has started (the old system’s support cannot end until the new system’s support has started).

Leads and lags adjust a dependency. A lag is a wait added after the predecessor: “FS + 2 days” after pouring concrete lets it cure; “wait 5 working days after sending the contract for signature”. A lead lets the successor start before the predecessor finishes: “FS − 3 days” means testing starts 3 days before the end of the build. Leads are one way to compress a schedule, but they add risk because the successor works on unfinished input.

Dependencies also differ by their origin. Mandatory dependencies come from the nature of the work (you cannot test code that does not exist). Discretionary dependencies are team choices or best practice (we prefer to finish the design before building), and they are the first ones to challenge when the schedule is too long. External dependencies sit outside the project: a vendor delivery, a regulator’s approval, another project’s release. External ones deserve a named contact and a place in the risk register.

Good networks have no “dangling” tasks: every activity except the start has a predecessor and every activity except the end has a successor. A task with no successor finishes in a void, and if it slips the schedule will not show any effect on the end date. Hard-coded start dates (constraints such as “must start on 3 March”) should be rare, because they stop the schedule from reacting to real changes.
points: FS: finish-to-start, the default; SS: start-to-start; FF: finish-to-finish; SF: start-to-finish (rare).
Lag = waiting time after the predecessor; lead = overlap, the successor starts early.
Mandatory, discretionary and external dependencies: challenge the discretionary ones first.
Every task except start and end needs a predecessor and a successor.
Avoid hard-coded dates: let the dependencies drive the schedule.

example.code:
ID  Activity           Duration  Predecessors
A   Requirements        5 d       -
B   Design             10 d       A (FS)
C   Build backend      15 d       B (FS)
D   Build frontend     12 d       B (FS)
E   Data migration      6 d       A (FS)
F   Testing             8 d       C, D, E (FS)
G   Go-live             1 d       F (FS)

        +--> E ---------------------+
        |                           v
Start-> A --> B --> C ------------> F --> G -> End
              |                     ^
              +---> D --------------+
example.note: The network used in the next lesson to find the critical path.

lessons.title: The critical path, float and the forward and backward pass
text: The critical path is the longest path through the network, from start to end. Its length is the shortest possible duration of the project: any delay on a critical activity delays the end date by the same amount, unless you act. Activities off the critical path have float (also called slack): time they can slip without moving the end date.

The forward pass computes, from the start, each activity’s early start (ES) and early finish (EF). Using day numbers where the project starts at day 0: EF = ES + duration, and an activity’s ES is the largest EF of its predecessors. In the network of the previous lesson: A 0–5, B 5–15, C 15–30, D 15–27, E 5–11; F waits for C, D and E, so ES = MAX(30, 27, 11) = 30 and EF = 38; G runs 38–39. The project takes 39 days.

The backward pass starts from the end and computes each activity’s late finish (LF) and late start (LS): LS = LF − duration, and an activity’s LF is the smallest LS of its successors. G: LF 39, LS 38. F: 30–38. C: LS 15. D: LF 30, LS 18. E: LF 30, LS 24. B: LF = MIN(15, 18) = 15, LS 5. A: LF = MIN(5, 24) = 5, LS 0.

Total float = LS − ES (or LF − EF). A, B, C, F and G have 0: they form the critical path A–B–C–F–G, 5 + 10 + 15 + 8 + 1 = 39 days. D has 3 days of total float, E has 19. Free float is the time an activity can slip without delaying the early start of any successor; here D’s free float is also 3 (F’s ES is 30, D finishes at 27). A path whose float is small, such as A–B–D–F–G with 3 days, is near-critical and must be watched: a 4-day slip on D creates a new critical path.

To shorten the critical path there are two classic schedule compression techniques. Crashing adds resources to critical activities (overtime, an extra developer) and costs money; it works only when the work can really be split. Fast-tracking runs in parallel activities that were planned in sequence (start the build before the design is fully signed), which costs little but adds risk of rework. Shortening a non-critical activity does nothing for the end date, a point interviewers like to test.
points: Critical path: the longest path; its length is the project duration.
Forward pass: ES = largest EF of predecessors; EF = ES + duration.
Backward pass: LF = smallest LS of successors; LS = LF − duration.
Total float = LS − ES; zero float means critical. Watch near-critical paths.
Compression: crashing (add resources, costs money), fast-tracking (overlap, adds risk).

example.code:
Act  Dur  ES  EF  LS  LF  Total float
A     5    0   5   0   5   0   critical
B    10    5  15   5  15   0   critical
C    15   15  30  15  30   0   critical
D    12   15  27  18  30   3
E     6    5  11  24  30  19
F     8   30  38  30  38   0   critical
G     1   38  39  38  39   0   critical

Critical path: A-B-C-F-G = 5+10+15+8+1 = 39 days
example.note: Forward pass fills ES and EF from the top; backward pass fills LF and LS from the end; float = LS − ES.

lessons.title: The Gantt chart, milestones and resource levelling
text: A Gantt chart draws each activity as a horizontal bar on a calendar, with the dependencies as arrows between bars. It is the most common way to show a schedule, because anyone can read it: what happens when, what overlaps, what is late. Most tools highlight the critical path in red. For a steering committee, a summary Gantt with the phases and milestones on one page is far more useful than 400 lines of tasks.

A milestone is a significant point or event with zero duration, drawn as a diamond: “design signed”, “UAT start”, “go-live”. Milestones are what sponsors track and what contracts often pay against. A good milestone is verifiable (a document signed, a system live), not vague (“design mostly done”). Many teams keep a short milestone list in the status report with baseline date, forecast date and status.

Resources turn a logical schedule into a realistic one. Assign people (or equipment) to each activity, then check the load: if the same developer is planned on C and D at 100 % during the same days, the plan is impossible. Resource levelling resolves such over-allocations by moving activities, first within their float; when there is not enough float, levelling pushes the end date. Resource smoothing, by contrast, only moves activities within their float and never changes the end date, so it may not remove every over-allocation.

Working days matter: tools schedule on a calendar with weekends, public holidays and people’s leave. A task of 10 working days that starts on a Monday finishes on the Friday of the following week. In French organisations, August holidays and the long weekends of May are classic traps for a plan built on a default calendar.

Tools: Microsoft Project is still the reference in many large companies for predictive schedules with dependencies, calendars and resources. Excel works for small projects and for analysis, but it does not compute dependencies by itself unless you build the formulas. Online tools such as Smartsheet, monday.com, Asana, Wrike or the timeline views in Jira are common in hybrid teams. The tool matters less than the logic: dependencies linked, no hard-coded dates, a baseline saved.
points: Gantt chart: bars on a calendar, dependencies as arrows, critical path highlighted.
Milestone: zero duration, verifiable, tracked by the sponsor.
Resource levelling may move the end date; resource smoothing stays within float.
Schedule on working days with holidays and leave.
MS Project, Excel or online tools: the logic matters more than the tool.

example.code:
Week:            1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
A Requirements   ■
B Design            ■  ■
C Build backend           ■  ■  ■          critical
D Build frontend          ■  ■  ■·         3 d float
E Data migration    ■  ■· ·  ·  ·          19 d float
F Testing                          ■  ■    critical
G Go-live                              ◆   milestone
(■ work, · float, ◆ milestone)

Over-allocation: same developer on C and D in weeks 4-5
Levelling: start D later, inside its 3 days of float first
example.note: Levelling uses float first; once the float is gone, the end date moves.

lessons.title: The baseline and tracking progress
text: The baseline is the approved version of the plan (scope, schedule and cost) that progress is measured against. Save it in the tool once the plan is agreed with the sponsor, before the work starts. Without a baseline, the plan is updated every week and the project is always “on time”, because nobody can see how far the dates have moved.

Track progress regularly, usually weekly: actual start and finish dates, the remaining duration of activities in progress and the forecast finish. Percent complete is a common measure, but it is easy to abuse: a task that is “90 % done” for three weeks is a well-known warning sign. Ask for the remaining duration instead, or use simple rules such as 0/100 (no credit until finished) or 50/50 (half at the start, half at the finish) for short tasks. For a group of tasks, weight percent complete by duration or effort: SUMPRODUCT(durations, percents) / SUM(durations).

Schedule variance in days compares forecast and baseline dates: baseline go-live day 39, forecast day 43, the project is 4 days late. Report it on milestones and on the end date, with the cause and the action. Earned value management measures schedule and cost performance together (SPI, CPI); it is covered in the project budget course, but expect interviewers to ask what an SPI below 1 means: less work done than planned by this date.

When a critical task slips, act in this order: confirm the new forecast with the person who does the work, check the impact on the critical path and the milestones, look at options (use float elsewhere, re-sequence, fast-track, crash, reduce scope through change control), then inform the sponsor with the options and your recommendation. A slip on a task with enough float is noted but does not need escalation.

Re-planning is normal; re-baselining is not done lightly. You update the forecast every week, but you change the baseline only after an approved change request (new scope, a new budget, a decision to move the go-live), so that the history of variances stays honest. Keep the old baseline in the tool for comparison, and record the reason in the change log.
points: Baseline: the approved plan, saved before the work starts.
Track actual dates, remaining duration and forecast finish every week.
Distrust “90 % done”; weight percent complete by duration or effort.
Schedule variance in days = forecast date − baseline date on milestones.
Re-plan weekly; re-baseline only after an approved change.

example.code:
A               B (Duration)  C (% complete)
1    Task            Duration      Complete
2    Requirements    10            100%
3    Design          5             60%
4    Build           8             25%
5    Testing         2             0%
6    Weighted        =SUMPRODUCT(B2:B5,C2:C5)/SUM(B2:B5)   -> 60%

Milestone   Baseline  Forecast  Variance (days)
Go-live     day 39    day 43    =43-39 -> 4 days late
example.note: Weighting by duration stops a small finished task from making the project look further along than it is.

items: Temporary endeavour that creates a unique product, service or result
Ongoing, repeated work that keeps the business running
Scope, time and cost move together
Plan up front, run in phases with phase gates
Predictive frame with agile delivery inside some phases
Formal go / no-go decision at the end of a phase
Why: options, costs, benefits, risks, recommendation
Authorises the project and names the PM; signed by the sponsor
Owns the business case, funds the project, takes the big decisions
Uncontrolled growth of scope without more time or budget
Deliverable-oriented breakdown of all the project work
The WBS holds all the work and nothing more
Lowest WBS level: estimable, one owner, trackable
Estimate from a similar past project
Visible project-level reserve for identified risks
Hidden margin added to each task estimate
Finish-to-start: B starts after A finishes
Start-to-start: B starts after A starts
Finish-to-finish: B finishes after A finishes
Start-to-finish: B finishes after A starts (rare)
Waiting time added after the predecessor
Overlap: the successor starts before the predecessor finishes
Longest path through the network; sets the project duration
Computes early start and early finish
Computes late finish and late start
LS − ES: slip allowed without moving the end date
Slip allowed without delaying any successor
Add resources to critical activities (costs money)
Run sequential activities in parallel (adds risk)
Activities as bars on a calendar
Removes over-allocation; may move the end date
Approved plan that progress is measured against

pitfalls: Starting the work without a signed charter: when scope or budget is disputed later, nothing shows what was agreed.
Forgetting the out-of-scope list, project management, testing or training in the scope and the WBS.
Typing dates into the schedule instead of linking tasks with dependencies, so a slip never shows its real impact.
Hiding padding in every task estimate instead of keeping honest estimates and a visible contingency reserve.
Trying to speed up the project by shortening non-critical tasks, which changes nothing to the end date.
Believing “90 % complete” for weeks instead of asking for the remaining duration.
Updating the baseline every week, which makes every project look on time and hides the real variance.

exercises.q: Excel: in E2, compute the PERT estimate (in days) of the task from its optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations.
exercises.hint: PERT weights the most likely value four times and divides by 6.
exercises.explain: (4 + 4 × 6 + 14) / 6 = 42 / 6 = 7 days. The estimate is above the most likely 6 days because the pessimistic tail (14) is long.

exercises.q: Excel, forward pass: D starts after both B and C have finished (finish-to-start). In D5, compute D’s earliest finish (day number).
exercises.hint: An activity starts when its last predecessor finishes: take the largest earliest finish, then add the duration.
exercises.explain: D’s early start is MAX(8, 7) = 8, so its early finish is 8 + 2 = 10. Using MAX makes the formula follow whichever predecessor finishes last.

exercises.q: Excel: in E4, compute task C’s total float in days from its late start and early start.
exercises.explain: 18 − 15 = 3 days: C can start up to 3 days late without moving the end date. A and B have 0 float: they are on the critical path.

exercises.q: Excel: the network has two paths, A–B–D and A–C–D. In D2, compute the length of the critical path in days (the longer of the two).
exercises.hint: Sum the durations of each path, then keep the longest.
exercises.explain: A–B–D = 5 + 10 + 4 = 19 days; A–C–D = 5 + 7 + 4 = 16 days. The critical path is A–B–D, 19 days, and C has 3 days of float.

exercises.q: Excel: in C6, compute the percent complete of the whole project, weighted by duration (as a decimal, e.g. 0.6).
exercises.hint: SUMPRODUCT multiplies each duration by its percent and adds them up; divide by the total duration.
exercises.explain: (10 × 1 + 5 × 0.6 + 8 × 0.25 + 2 × 0) / 25 = 15 / 25 = 0.6, so 60 %. A simple average of the four percents would give 46 %, because it gives the 2-day task as much weight as the 10-day one.

exercises.q: Put the planning steps of a predictive project in order.
steps: Write the business case and get the charter signed
Collect requirements and write the scope statement
Break the scope down into a WBS
Estimate the work packages and their activities
Link the activities with dependencies and find the critical path
Agree the plan with the sponsor and save the baseline
exercises.answer: Why and authority first (business case, charter), then what (scope, WBS), then how long (estimates), then in which order (dependencies, critical path), then who (resources), and finally the approved baseline that progress is measured against.

exercises.q: Sort these items: which belong in the project charter, and which in the detailed project plan?
exercises.answer: The charter authorises the project at a high level and is signed by the sponsor; the detailed plan (WBS, schedule, resources, baseline) is built afterwards by the project manager and the team.

exercises.q: Match each dependency type with an example.
pairs: User acceptance tests start when system tests are finished
Writing the user guide can begin once the build has begun
The test report cannot be finished until testing is finished
Support of the old system cannot end until support of the new one has started
exercises.answer: FS is the default and by far the most used; SS and FF let work overlap; SF is rare, mostly for handovers between an old and a new service.

exercises.q: Week 5: the developer tells you the billing API integration, a critical-path activity, will take 6 days longer than planned. Go-live is in 7 weeks.

choices.label: Confirm the new estimate and its cause, then update the schedule to see the impact on milestones and the end date
choices.feedback: You need a reliable forecast before deciding anything: on the critical path, 6 days late means go-live 6 days late unless you act.

choices.label: Tell the developer to work weekends so the plan does not change
choices.feedback: Imposing overtime before understanding the cause rarely works, burns the team out and hides the problem from the sponsor.

choices.label: Move the go-live date by 6 days in the baseline
choices.feedback: The baseline changes only after an approved change. Update the forecast, not the baseline.

steps.text: The forecast shows go-live 6 days late. Which options do you prepare?

choices.label: Fast-track UAT preparation in parallel, add a second developer to the integration (crash), or move a low-priority feature to phase 2, each with cost and risk
choices.feedback: Options on the critical path, with their cost and risk, let the sponsor make an informed choice.

choices.label: Shorten the training task, which has 15 days of float
choices.feedback: Shortening a non-critical task does nothing for the end date.

choices.label: Cut testing by 6 days to keep the date
choices.feedback: Cutting tests silently moves the risk into production; at most it is an option to present openly, with its risk.

steps.text: How do you inform the sponsor?

choices.label: Now, with the variance, the cause, the options and your recommendation
choices.feedback: Early bad news with options keeps trust; the sponsor decides, and an approved change is recorded and, if needed, re-baselined.

choices.label: Wait for the next monthly steering committee in three weeks
choices.feedback: Three weeks lost: by then some options (fast-tracking, extra staff) may no longer be possible.

exercises.answer: Confirm the forecast, measure the impact on the critical path, prepare options (fast-tracking, crashing, scope through change control) with their costs and risks, and escalate early with a recommendation. Change the baseline only after an approved change.

exercises.q: The sponsor wants the project finished two weeks earlier. Which action can actually shorten the project?
options: Assign an extra developer to a task with 12 days of float
Overlap two critical activities that were planned in sequence (fast-tracking)
exercises.answer: Only work on the critical path changes the end date. Fast-tracking two critical activities shortens it, at the price of a higher risk of rework; extra staff on a task with float changes nothing.

exercises.q: Task X has: early start day 12, early finish day 20, late start day 16, late finish day 24. What is its total float, in days?
exercises.answer: Total float = LS − ES = 16 − 12 = 4 days (or LF − EF = 24 − 20 = 4). X is not critical: it can slip 4 days without moving the end date.

exercises.q: Write a WBS (three levels) for organising a one-day company conference for 150 people. Then name two items you would put out of scope.
exercises.answer: 1 Company conference. 1.1 Project management (plan, budget, status meetings, supplier contracts). 1.2 Programme (agenda; speakers booked and briefed; presentations collected). 1.3 Venue (venue booked; room layout and AV equipment; accessibility and safety check). 1.4 Catering (menu chosen including dietary needs; coffee breaks; lunch). 1.5 Attendees (invitation; registration site; badges; reminders). 1.6 Communication (internal announcement; event page; photos after the event). 1.7 On-the-day operations (run sheet, staff and welcome desk, set-up and dismantling). 1.8 Closure (feedback survey, supplier invoices, lessons learned). Each level-3 item is a work package with one owner. Out of scope, for example: travel and hotel booking for attendees, an evening party, live streaming. The 100 % check: if all of these are done, the conference has happened and been closed.

interview.q: Walk me through how you build a project schedule.
interview.a: I start from the signed charter and the scope, and break the scope into a WBS down to work packages with one owner each. With the people doing the work, I list the activities, estimate them (analogous early, three-point for uncertain tasks) and link them with dependencies, mostly finish-to-start. Then I find the critical path and float, assign resources and level them on a real calendar with holidays, and add milestones. I review it with the team and the sponsor, add a visible contingency reserve, and save the baseline before the work starts.

interview.q: What is the critical path, and why does it matter?
interview.a: It is the longest sequence of dependent activities from start to end, so it sets the shortest possible project duration. Any delay on it moves the end date unless we act, so it is where I focus tracking and where schedule compression must happen. I also watch near-critical paths with little float, because a small slip there can create a new critical path.

interview.q: A stakeholder asks for “a small extra feature” halfway through. What do you do?
interview.a: I do not say yes or no on the spot. I log it as a change request, assess the impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk with the team, and take it to the sponsor or change board with options: add it with more time or budget, swap it for something of equal size, or plan it for a later phase. Accepting small changes informally is how scope creep starts.

interview.q: How do you estimate a task you have never done before?
interview.a: I ask the people who will do it, look for an analogous piece of work, and use three-point estimates: optimistic, most likely and pessimistic, combined with PERT (O + 4M + P) / 6. I record the assumptions, give a range rather than one number, keep the uncertainty visible in a contingency reserve instead of padding each task, and plan to re-estimate once we know more, for example after a short spike or prototype.

interview.q: What is the difference between total float and free float?
interview.a: Total float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project end date: late start minus early start. Free float is how long it can slip without delaying the early start of any successor. An activity can have total float but no free float, if its successor shares the same float; using it then eats into the successor’s margin.

interview.q: Your project is two weeks behind. How do you recover?
interview.a: First I confirm the real forecast and the cause. Then I look only at the critical path: fast-track activities that can overlap, crash where extra people genuinely speed up the work, remove discretionary dependencies, use float elsewhere to free resources, or reduce scope through change control. I present the options with cost and risk to the sponsor with a recommendation, and I change the baseline only if a change is approved.

interview.q: Waterfall or agile: which do you prefer?
interview.a: It depends on the project. With stable requirements, hard dependencies, a fixed contract or regulatory dates, a predictive plan with phase gates works well. When users need to react to early versions, agile iterations reduce the risk of building the wrong thing. Many of my projects are hybrid: fixed milestones and a budget, with sprints for the software part. What matters is choosing deliberately and being transparent about the plan.

interview.q: What is a baseline and when would you change it?
interview.a: It is the approved scope, schedule and cost that I measure progress against, saved before execution starts. I update the forecast every week, but I re-baseline only after an approved change request, such as new scope or a sponsor decision to move go-live, and I keep the old baseline and the reason, so the variance history stays honest.
